content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses identify 'justify/justification' primarily as God's forensic (courtroom) declaration that a sinner is righteous — acquitted and placed in right standing with God — through faith in Christ apart from works of the law, typically involving the imputation of Christ's righteousness. All also list alternatives: Catholic transformative infusion, New Perspective covenant-membership verdict, Orthodox participation/theosis, and a demonstrative/vindication sense (James 2, Matt 11:19, Luke 7:29) in which works or deeds prove righteousness.","book_summary":"The book defines justify broadly as to judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a charge (the opposite of condemn), applying to God, wisdom, and human deeds as well as sinners. It affirms that God justifies the sinner, but specifies the mechanism as forgiveness in Christ — God does not declare wrongdoing right. Its common-view note explicitly flags the once-for-all imputation-of-Christ's-righteousness-through-faith-apart-from-works formulation as the 'commonly taught' view it is distinguishing itself from.","consensus_core_identification":"Justification = God's legal/declarative act of counting a believing sinner righteous, grounded in Christ's work and classically explicated via imputed righteousness received by faith apart from works.","book_core_identification":"Justification = the generic judicial act of declaring or demonstrating anyone or anything right against a charge; God's justification of sinners is accomplished specifically through forgiveness in Christ, not by imputing a righteousness that calls wrong right, and it accommodates demonstrative justification by works (James 2).","core_relation":"BOOK_BROADENS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUPERSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book broadens the term's extension beyond the soteriological case to any vindication against a charge (judges justifying the righteous, people justifying God, wisdom justified of her children, Abraham and Rahab justified by works), cases the consensus treats as secondary or alternative senses. Within the soteriological case, it shifts the ground from imputation of Christ's righteousness to forgiveness/remission (Rom 4:7-8), and it appears to fold James's justification-by-works into the same definition rather than harmonizing it away as merely 'demonstrative' of a prior forensic verdict.","material_contradiction":"No outright contradiction of the consensus core: the book retains a declarative/judicial referent and affirms that God justifies the believing sinner in Christ. Its implicit rejection of the 'once-for-all imputation' mechanic disputes the classic Protestant explication (one listed consensus formulation), but this is a boundary/mechanism dispute, not replacement of the central referent, and forgiveness-based readings and demonstrative senses already appear within the consensus responses' alternatives.","rationale":"Both the consensus and the book identify justification as a judicial declaring-right that is the opposite of condemnation, with God as the one who justifies the ungodly through Christ. The book, however, materially widens the term to all vindication contexts, elevates the demonstrative sense (Matt 11:19; Luke 7:29; Jas 2) from an 'alternative' to part of the primary definition, and reframes the mechanism as forgiveness rather than imputed righteousness — explicitly setting itself against the 'commonly taught' imputation formula. That is real disagreement at the boundary and mechanism while preserving the consensus's general category, which fits REFINED rather than MATCH or DIVERGENT.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for DIVERGENT: by flagging the imputation-through-faith-apart-from-works formulation as merely 'commonly taught' and substituting forgiveness as the operative mechanism (while endorsing James's 'justified by works, and not by faith only'), the book arguably contradicts the consensus's central Protestant identification rather than refining it. This is mitigated because the consensus responses themselves list forgiveness-adjacent, transformative, and demonstrative readings as recognized alternatives, and Rom 4:6-8 itself links imputed righteousness to forgiveness, so the book's core remains within the recognized declarative category.","confidence":"medium"}
